# Espresso Machine

## Setup

I run a 58 mm basket on the double spout, dosing 18 g of medium roast into a level bed and tamping flat with a calibrated tamper. The PID sits at 93 C, which keeps the brew water stable across back to back shots. Pressure reads 9 bar at the group with the pump running against a blank disc, and I check that gauge every couple of months because it drifts slowly. The grind lands fine enough that a 25 second pull gives roughly 36 g in the cup. Preheating the cup and the portafilter makes a difference I can taste, so I start the kettle for the mug before I weigh beans. The reservoir gets refilled with filtered water, mainly to slow scale buildup. I keep a small notebook of dose, grind and time for each new bag of beans, which makes dialling in quicker when the roast changes.

## Cleaning

Every Sunday I flush the group with a blind basket and a scoop of detergent, running several short cycles until the waste water comes out clear. A citric solution goes through the boiler circuit once every three months, which means dissolving two tablespoons in a litre of warm water and letting it stand for half an hour. The shower screen comes off for a soak in the same solution, and a soft brush works the rubber gasket where old grounds collect. The drip tray gets a rinse and a wipe with a damp cloth, and the portafilter basket is scrubbed with a stiff nylon brush. I dry everything before it goes back so nothing corrodes at the seams.

## Troubleshooting

Channeling shows up as a fast blond gusher and a puck with a crater in the middle, usually a distribution problem rather than a burr problem. Sour shots mean the water is not hot enough or the grind is too coarse, so I nudge the PID up one degree or tighten the setting a notch. A rattling pump noise on start up is often air in the line from a low reservoir. If the lever feels stiff, the cam needs a smear of food safe grease. Weak, watery shots with a pale crema usually point at stale beans rather than the gear.
